title: 2 Chronicles 12:1–12
context: Once Rehoboam is established and strong, he and all Israel abandon the LORD’s law. In his fifth year Shishak king of Egypt invades with a large army, takes Judah’s fortified cities, and comes to Jerusalem, “because they had trespassed against the LORD” (12:2). Shemaiah announces that because they have forsaken the LORD, the LORD has left them to Shishak. The princes and the king humble themselves and confess, “The LORD is righteous,” and the LORD grants partial deliverance: Jerusalem will not be destroyed, but Judah will serve Shishak, to learn the difference between serving God and serving the kingdoms of the earth (12:5–8). Shishak carries off the treasures of the temple and palace, including Solomon’s gold shields, which Rehoboam replaces with bronze. The parallel is 1 Kings 14:25–28, which reports the plunder but not Shemaiah’s message or the humbling; 1 Kings 14:22–24 describes Judah’s sins in more detail. Both traditions read the unit as shared ground: sin brings real discipline, humbling brings real but limited relief, and God remains righteous.

verses.text: When the kingdom of Rehoboam was established and he was strong, he abandoned the LORD’s law, and all Israel with him.
verses.arminianNotes: Once Rehoboam is established and strong, he abandons the LORD’s law, and all Israel with him. Arminian readers see a real and culpable turning away. Security became an occasion for complacency, and the king led his people into unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the danger of prosperity, which can lead the heart away from God. 1 Kings 14:22–24 describes Judah’s sins in more detail. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober warning that strength received from God must not become a reason to forget him.

verses.text: In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem, because they had trespassed against the LORD,
verses.arminianNotes: In Rehoboam’s fifth year, Shishak king of Egypt comes against Jerusalem “because they had trespassed against the LORD.” Arminian readers note that the Chronicler links the invasion to Judah’s unfaithfulness, a consequence of their own choices.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God using a foreign king to discipline his people. 1 Kings 14:25 reports the invasion without stating the reason. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as connecting sin and discipline, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 14:25, and neither builds on extrabiblical reconstructions of Shishak’s campaign.

verses.text: with twelve hundred chariots and sixty thousand horsemen. The people were without number who came with him out of Egypt: the Lubim, the Sukkiim, and the Ethiopians.
verses.arminianNotes: Shishak comes with 1,200 chariots, 60,000 horsemen, and countless troops, including Lubim, Sukkiim, and Ethiopians. Arminian readers note the overwhelming size of the army facing Judah. The numbers stress how helpless Judah was without the LORD’s protection.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the vast army as underlining Judah’s vulnerability once it had forsaken God. Shared ground: both traditions read the figures as part of the historical account, decline to build conclusions on the numbers, and see the point in Judah’s need for God’s help.

verses.text: He took the fortified cities which belonged to Judah, and came to Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes: Shishak takes Judah’s fortified cities and comes to Jerusalem. Arminian readers note the bitter irony: the cities Rehoboam had carefully fortified (11:5–12) fall to the invader. Human preparation cannot protect a people who have turned from God.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the futility of fortifications without faithfulness. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober reminder that security rests finally with the LORD, and that the strength described in chapter 11 offered no defense once Judah abandoned his law.

verses.text: Now Shemaiah the prophet came to Rehoboam and to the princes of Judah, who were gathered together to Jerusalem because of Shishak, and said to them, “The LORD says, ‘You have forsaken me, therefore I have also left you in the hand of Shishak.’ ”
verses.arminianNotes: Shemaiah tells Rehoboam and the princes, “You have forsaken me, therefore I have also left you in the hand of Shishak.” Arminian readers note the correspondence between Judah’s action and God’s response. Their choice to forsake God has real consequences.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see God’s righteous judgment declared through his prophet, with the invasion as his appointed discipline. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a clear statement that forsaking God brings judgment, and both see in the prophetic word an invitation to repentance.

verses.text: Then the princes of Israel and the king humbled themselves; and they said, “The LORD is righteous.”
verses.arminianNotes: The princes and the king humble themselves and say, “The LORD is righteous.” Arminian readers see genuine repentance freely offered. The leaders accept God’s verdict and acknowledge their guilt, which opens the way for mercy.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers see the same confession as the right response to God’s word, and they see God’s grace at work in bringing the leaders to humility. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a model of humbling oneself before God, acknowledging his justice, and seeking his mercy.

verses.text: When the LORD saw that they humbled themselves, the LORD’s word came to Shemaiah, saying, “They have humbled themselves. I will not destroy them, but I will grant them some deliverance, and my wrath won’t be poured out on Jerusalem by the hand of Shishak.
verses.arminianNotes: When the LORD sees they have humbled themselves, he promises not to destroy them but to grant some deliverance. Arminian readers note God’s real responsiveness to repentance. Mercy follows humility, and the outcome changes because the people turn.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s mercy toward the humble and note that his response fits his revealed character. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that God hears those who humble themselves, and both note that the relief is partial, not a full restoration.

verses.text: Nevertheless they will be his servants, that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries.”
verses.arminianNotes: Yet Judah will serve Shishak, “that they may know my service, and the service of the kingdoms of the countries.” Arminian readers see a lesson learned through experience: serving foreign kings will show how much better it is to serve the LORD.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s discipline as instructive, teaching his people the difference between his service and the service of others. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as purposeful discipline, in which God allows lasting consequences in order to teach his people.

verses.text: So Shishak king of Egypt came up against Jerusalem and took away the treasures of the LORD’s house and the treasures of the king’s house. He took it all away. He also took away the shields of gold which Solomon had made.
verses.arminianNotes: Shishak takes the treasures of the LORD’s house and the king’s house, including Solomon’s gold shields. Arminian readers see the loss of Solomon’s glory within a few years, a warning about how quickly blessings can be squandered through unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers note that the wealth God gave Solomon is stripped away in one generation. Outward splendor cannot protect a people who have turned from God. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as the cost of Judah’s sin, consistent with the notes on 1 Kings 14:26.

verses.text: King Rehoboam made shields of bronze in their place, and committed them to the hands of the captains of the guard, who kept the door of the king’s house.
verses.arminianNotes: Rehoboam makes bronze shields to replace the gold ones and commits them to the guards of the palace door. Arminian readers note the poignant substitution. The bronze shields keep up appearances, but the loss of glory is plain to all.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see the replacement as a sign of diminished glory under judgment. The same detail appears in 1 Kings 14:27. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as a sober picture of what Judah lost, without allegorizing the shields beyond the narrative’s point.

verses.text: As often as the king entered into the LORD’s house, the guard came and bore them, then brought them back into the guard room.
verses.arminianNotes: Whenever the king enters the LORD’s house, the guards carry the shields and then return them to the guard room. Arminian readers note that royal ceremony continues, though diminished. The routine reminds readers of what had been lost through unfaithfulness.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see continuing worship and ceremony in a humbled kingdom. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as historical description that underlines the loss of Solomon’s splendor while noting that the king still went to the LORD’s house.

verses.text: When he humbled himself, the LORD’s wrath turned from him, so as not to destroy him altogether. Moreover, there were good things found in Judah.
verses.arminianNotes: When Rehoboam humbles himself, the LORD’s wrath turns from him, and there are good things in Judah. Arminian readers see repentance bringing real relief. God’s response to humility spares Judah from complete destruction.
verses.reformedNotes: Reformed readers likewise see God’s mercy toward the humble and the preservation of good things in Judah. Shared ground: both traditions read the verse as showing that humility before God brings real but limited relief, and both note that the Chronicler records some good in Judah alongside its failures.
